content: The designations and presentation of material in this publication do not reflect any opinion by the World Health Organization (WHO) regarding the legal status of any country, territory, city, or area, or its authorities, nor do they imply any judgment on the delimitation of its frontiers or boundaries. Dotted lines on maps represent approximate borderlines where full agreement may not yet exist. The mention of specific companies or manufacturers’ products does not imply endorsement or recommendation by WHO over others of a similar nature that are not mentioned. Proprietary product names are distinguished by initial capital letters, except for errors and omissions. WHO has taken all reasonable precautions to verify the information in this publication. However, the material is distributed without any warranty, either express or implied. The responsibility for interpretation and use of the material lies with the reader. After the conclusion of pilot tests conducted in 2007 and 2008, a revised version of these guidelines will be published. In the event of new epidemics or pandemics, additional recommendations will be provided. The purpose of this document is to provide infection control guidance to prevent the transmission of acute infectious respiratory diseases during healthcare delivery, with a focus on diseases that may constitute a public health emergency of international concern as defined in the International Health Regulations (2005). Healthcare facility managers may also use this guidance to prepare for epidemics and pandemics. This document is intended for use by government planners, healthcare facility administrators, infection control professionals, occupational health specialists, other professionals involved in patient care, and direct care providers. The infection control advice is based on available information about the main routes of pathogen transmission and aims to provide guidance for continuous and sustainable improvements in healthcare safety. These guidelines offer Member States a conceptual framework for adaptation according to local regulations, settings, needs, and resources. Healthcare facilities are encouraged to review and adapt the recommendations accordingly. The guidelines were developed following a systematic review of scientific literature identified through PubMed and the Cochrane Library, as well as secondary papers in English, Chinese, French, Portuguese, and Spanish. International and national infection control guidelines and textbooks were also consulted. The document underwent internal and external peer reviews. The Guideline Steering Group evaluated reviewers' comments, provided guidance when opinions differed, and oversaw the incorporation of amendments and finalization of the document. Pilot tests of the guidelines were conducted in 2007 and 2008 in each of the six WHO regions to provide local data on the document's clarity, resource requirements, feasibility, and validity of the interventions. These tests also helped inform implementation and dissemination strategies. The guidelines will be reviewed and updated after the pilot tests. Knowledge about modes of transmission of respiratory diseases is rapidly evolving. Case surveillance and investigation of cases and contacts are critical for defining and identifying changes in the epidemiology of human infections and will continue to inform infection control recommendations. Modifications to these guidelines will be made as additional information becomes available. The document is the result of collaborative efforts across WHO, led by the Department of Communicable Disease Surveillance and Response at the WHO Regional Office for the Western Pacific and the Department of Epidemic and Pandemic Alert and Response at WHO Headquarters, with significant input from staff at other WHO regional offices and many partners worldwide.
